6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: OpenCV loads images as NumPy arrays of shape (H, W, 3) with uint8 values 0-255, but orders channels as Blue-Green-Red (BGR) instead of the RGB order used by PIL, matplotlib, and almost every deep learning framework.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: A historical legacy from OpenCV's origins in early-2000s Intel computer vision work, where BGR matched the byte layout of Windows BMP files and common camera/codec hardware of the era. The convention stuck for backward compatibility even as the rest of the ecosystem standardized on RGB.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.imread() returns a (H,W,3) BGR array; cv2.imwrite() expects BGR on write; grayscale images are (H,W) with no channel axis. cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB) swaps channel order for display or for handing off to RGB-expecting code.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Whenever reading, writing, or doing pixel-level array manipulation with OpenCV functions — np.array operations, slicing, channel splitting (cv2.split) all work directly on the BGR array.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Don't pass a raw cv2.imread() array straight into matplotlib's imshow, PIL, or an RGB-trained model without converting first — colors will be visibly wrong (blue/red swapped) or accuracy will silently degrade.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: The single most common OpenCV bug for beginners: plt.imshow(cv2.imread('img.jpg')) shows a blue-tinted image because matplotlib assumes RGB. Worse, feeding BGR pixels into an RGB-trained classifier doesn't crash — it just quietly tanks accuracy because R and B channels are swapped.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: img = cv2.imread('photo.jpg') gives shape (480,640,3) in BGR; img[0,0] might be [200,150,100] (B=200,G=150,R=100); plt.imshow(cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)) is required to display it with correct colors.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: Different mathematical representations of color: BGR/RGB encode color as additive red/green/blue intensities; HSV separates Hue (color), Saturation (intensity of color), and Value (brightness); LAB separates perceptual Lightness from two color-opponent axes (a: green-red, b: blue-yellow); Grayscale collapses to a single luminance channel.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: RGB/BGR is how sensors and displays capture/render light, but it tangles color and brightness together, making color-based segmentation hard (a red object under dim light has very different RGB values than under bright light). HSV and LAB decouple illumination from chromaticity, and grayscale exists because many CV algorithms (edges, features, OCR) don't need color at all and run faster on one channel.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV) maps RGB cube coordinates onto a cylindrical hue/saturation/value space; cv2.COLOR_BGR2LAB maps to the CIE LAB perceptual space; cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY applies a weighted sum (roughly 0.299R+0.587G+0.114B) to collapse channels.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Use HSV for color-based thresholding/masking that should be robust to lighting changes (e.g., 'find all red pixels'); use LAB when you need perceptually uniform color differences (e.g., color correction, comparing color similarity); use grayscale for edge detection, feature matching, and most OCR preprocessing where color carries no information.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Don't threshold directly in RGB for color detection — a single 'red' object can have wildly different RGB triples under different lighting, making RGB thresholds brittle. Don't convert to grayscale before tasks that genuinely need color (e.g., distinguishing a ripe vs unripe tomato).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: Hue in OpenCV's HSV wraps around at 180 (not 360, since uint8 caps at 255) — red spans both ends of the hue range (0-10 and 170-180), so a naive single-range threshold for 'red' misses half the red pixels. People also forget OpenCV's HSV range is H:0-179, S:0-255, V:0-255, not the 0-360/0-100/0-100 ranges shown in online color pickers.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: To detect a red traffic cone: convert to HSV, then combine two masks — cv2.inRange(hsv,(0,100,100),(10,255,255)) OR cv2.inRange(hsv,(170,100,100),(180,255,255)) — because red wraps around hue=0/180.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: Basic spatial operations that change an image's dimensions or orientation: resize (cv2.resize) changes pixel dimensions via interpolation; crop is plain NumPy slicing; rotate (cv2.rotate or cv2.getRotationMatrix2D + cv2.warpAffine) rotates around a center point; flip (cv2.flip) mirrors horizontally/vertically.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: Models require fixed input sizes, datasets need augmentation for robustness, and real-world images arrive at arbitrary orientations/sizes — these transforms are the basic toolkit for normalizing and augmenting image data before any higher-level processing.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.resize(img,(w,h),interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR/INTER_AREA/INTER_CUBIC) resamples pixels; cropping is img[y1:y2, x1:x2] since images are just arrays; rotation builds a 2x3 affine matrix M=cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center,angle,scale) and applies it with cv2.warpAffine(img,M,(w,h)); cv2.flip(img,0/1/-1) flips vertically/horizontally/both.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Resize for feeding fixed-size model inputs or thumbnailing; crop for ROI extraction after detection; rotate for deskewing scanned documents or data augmentation; flip for augmentation (horizontal flips are safe for most natural images, vertical flips usually aren't for text/faces).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Avoid cv2.INTER_NEAREST for downscaling photos (aliasing/jagged edges — use INTER_AREA); avoid flipping images containing text or asymmetric semantic content (a flipped 'EXIT' sign or digit '6'→'9' breaks meaning) unless the task is rotation/flip-invariant.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: cv2.resize takes (width,height) but NumPy shape is (height,width,channels) — mixing these up silently produces a stretched/squished image with no error. Also, warpAffine rotation around the image center can crop corners off the rotated image unless the output canvas size is recomputed to fit the rotated bounding box.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: Rotating a scanned receipt by 5 degrees to deskew: M = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((w/2,h/2), 5, 1.0); rotated = cv2.warpAffine(img, M, (w,h)) — corners of the original rectangle now fall outside the (w,h) canvas and get clipped unless the canvas is enlarged.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: A smoothing filter that convolves the image with a 2D Gaussian kernel, replacing each pixel with a weighted average of its neighbors where weights fall off with distance according to a Gaussian (bell curve) — the standard first-line technique for removing high-frequency noise.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: Sensor noise, compression artifacts, and fine texture create high-frequency variations that confuse downstream algorithms (edge detectors fire on noise, not real edges; thresholding becomes unstable). Gaussian blur suppresses these high frequencies while preserving lower-frequency structure (overall shapes, large edges).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.GaussianBlur(img,(k,k),sigma) convolves the image with a kxk Gaussian kernel; larger kernel size or sigma = more smoothing. The kernel is separable (a 2D Gaussian = outer product of two 1D Gaussians), so OpenCV applies it as two fast 1D convolutions internally.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: As a preprocessing step before edge detection (Canny explicitly recommends a Gaussian pre-blur), thresholding, or any pipeline sensitive to pixel-level noise; also used to create image pyramids and as part of unsharp masking.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Avoid heavy blurring before tasks needing fine detail (OCR character recognition, small-feature keypoint detection) — blur destroys exactly the high-frequency information those tasks rely on. Avoid using it as a substitute for proper denoising on heavily corrupted images (use bilateral or non-local means instead, which preserve edges).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: An odd kernel size is required (cv2.GaussianBlur errors or behaves oddly with even sizes); too large a kernel blurs away the actual object edges you wanted to detect, causing Canny/Sobel to miss real boundaries; sigma=0 lets OpenCV auto-compute sigma from kernel size, which surprises people expecting it to mean 'no blur'.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: Standard Canny preprocessing: blurred = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray,(5,5),1.4) before cv2.Canny(blurred,50,150) — without this step, Canny produces a noisy mess of spurious edge fragments from sensor noise.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: An automatic global thresholding method that finds the single pixel-intensity threshold which best separates a grayscale image's histogram into two classes (foreground/background) by maximizing between-class variance (equivalently minimizing within-class variance).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: Manually picking a threshold value (e.g., 'everything below 127 is black') is fragile — it breaks the moment lighting changes. Otsu's method derives the threshold directly from the image's own histogram, so it adapts automatically to each image's brightness distribution, assuming a roughly bimodal histogram (distinct foreground and background intensity peaks).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU) ignores the supplied threshold value (0), computes the image histogram, and exhaustively tests every possible threshold t to find the one that maximizes the variance between the two resulting pixel classes — an O(256) search over 8-bit intensity levels.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Document scanning/binarization where text is reliably darker than background, simple foreground/background separation under fairly uniform lighting, and as a quick automatic baseline before trying more complex segmentation.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Avoid when lighting is uneven across the image (a shadow on one side of a document) — a single global threshold can't handle spatially varying brightness; avoid when the histogram isn't bimodal (e.g., textured/cluttered backgrounds with no clear intensity separation) — Otsu will pick a threshold that doesn't correspond to any meaningful boundary.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: On a photo of a document with a shadow gradient, Otsu picks one global threshold that correctly binarizes the bright half but turns the shadowed half entirely black (or vice versa), destroying text in that region — the classic motivation for switching to adaptive thresholding.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: _, binary = cv2.threshold(gray, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY+cv2.THRESH_OTSU) on a scanned page with uniform lighting cleanly separates black text from white paper without any manual tuning.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: A thresholding technique that computes a different threshold for each pixel based on the intensity statistics of a local neighborhood around it (mean or Gaussian-weighted mean minus a constant C), rather than one global threshold for the whole image.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: Global thresholds (even Otsu's optimal one) fail when illumination varies across the image — a single threshold can't be correct for both a brightly lit and a shadowed region. Adaptive thresholding fixes this by letting the 'local background level' vary across the image.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.adaptiveThreshold(gray,255,cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C,cv2.THRESH_BINARY,blockSize,C) slides a blockSize x blockSize window over the image; for each pixel, computes the local mean (or Gaussian-weighted mean) of that window, subtracts constant C, and uses the result as that pixel's threshold.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Binarizing photographed documents/whiteboards with uneven lighting or shadows, scanning receipts taken with a phone camera, any scenario where the 'paper white' level varies spatially.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Avoid on images with uniform lighting where Otsu works fine and is cheaper/simpler; avoid very small blockSize (creates noisy, speckled binarization) or very large blockSize (degenerates toward global thresholding and loses the local adaptivity benefit).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: Choosing blockSize too small makes the threshold too locally reactive — it can binarize noise as if it were structure, producing salt-and-pepper artifacts inside what should be uniform regions. The constant C also needs tuning per use case; a wrong sign or magnitude can invert which regions become foreground.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: binary = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(gray,255,cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C,cv2.THRESH_BINARY,11,2) reliably binarizes a phone photo of a whiteboard with a glare spot, where Otsu's single threshold would either blow out the glare region to white or crush the rest to black.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: A family of operations on binary (or grayscale) images that probe the image with a small shape called a structuring element (kernel): erosion shrinks white regions (removes small white noise, thins shapes), dilation grows white regions (fills small holes, thickens shapes), opening = erosion then dilation (removes small noise specks while preserving overall shape), closing = dilation then erosion (fills small holes/gaps while preserving overall shape).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: Thresholding rarely produces perfectly clean binary masks — there's salt-and-pepper noise, small holes inside objects, or thin bridges connecting objects that shouldn't be connected. Morphological operations clean up these artifacts using simple, fast, geometry-based rules rather than statistical filtering.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.erode(img,kernel) sets a pixel to foreground only if ALL pixels under the kernel are foreground (shrinks); cv2.dilate(img,kernel) sets a pixel to foreground if ANY pixel under the kernel is foreground (grows); cv2.morphologyEx(img,cv2.MORPH_OPEN,kernel) and cv2.MORPH_CLOSE chain erode+dilate or dilate+erode respectively.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Cleaning up binarized document images before OCR (opening removes speckle noise, closing fills broken character strokes), separating touching objects (erosion), or connecting nearby fragments of the same object (dilation/closing) before contour detection.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Avoid aggressive morphology on images where fine structure matters (thin text strokes, small features) — erosion can delete thin characters entirely, dilation can merge adjacent characters into illegible blobs. Avoid using morphology as a substitute for proper segmentation when objects genuinely overlap.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: Using too large a kernel or too many iterations causes opening to erase small-but-meaningful objects entirely (small text, thin lines), or closing to fuse genuinely separate objects (merging adjacent characters or nearby people in a crowd mask) into one connected component, breaking downstream contour/counting logic.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: After Otsu thresholding a noisy document scan, cv2.morphologyEx(binary,cv2.MORPH_OPEN,np.ones((2,2),np.uint8)) removes isolated noise pixels, and cv2.morphologyEx(binary,cv2.MORPH_CLOSE,np.ones((3,3),np.uint8)) reconnects characters whose strokes got fragmented by the threshold.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: Contrast-enhancement techniques that redistribute pixel intensities to span the full available range. Global histogram equalization remaps the entire image's intensity histogram to be approximately uniform; CLAHE (Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization) does this locally on small tiles with a clip limit to prevent over-amplification.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: Low-contrast images (underexposed photos, medical scans, hazy/foggy images) concentrate pixel values in a narrow range, making details hard to see for both humans and algorithms. Global equalization fixes overall contrast, but can over-amplify noise in flat regions and wash out local detail in images with both bright and dark areas — CLAHE addresses this by working tile-by-tile with a clipped histogram.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.equalizeHist(gray) computes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of pixel intensities and remaps each intensity to spread the CDF uniformly across 0-255. cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit, tileGridSize) divides the image into tiles, equalizes each tile's histogram (clipping bins above clipLimit to avoid over-boosting noise), then bilinearly interpolates tile boundaries to avoid blocky artifacts.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Enhancing underexposed/overexposed photos before feature detection or display, improving contrast in medical imaging (X-rays, CT) where CLAHE is a standard preprocessing step, or any image where important detail is compressed into a narrow intensity band.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Avoid global equalizeHist on images with both very bright and very dark regions in a single frame (it can over-enhance noise in flat areas while not helping the regions that actually need it) — prefer CLAHE there. Avoid applying either to already well-exposed images, as it can introduce unnatural-looking contrast and amplify compression artifacts.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: Global histogram equalization on an image with a large uniform region (e.g., sky, or a dark background) dramatically amplifies subtle noise in that region into visible banding/artifacts, because equalization stretches even tiny intensity variations across a wide output range. CLAHE with too small a clip limit under-enhances; too large a clip limit approaches plain (noisy) global equalization.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0, tileGridSize=(8,8)); enhanced = clahe.apply(gray) is the standard first step in many medical imaging pipelines (e.g., enhancing chest X-rays) to reveal detail in both dense bone and soft tissue regions simultaneously.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: A nonlinear point operation that remaps pixel intensities according to output = 255 * (input/255)^gamma, where gamma < 1 brightens (especially shadows/midtones) and gamma > 1 darkens — used to correct for the nonlinear relationship between stored pixel values and perceived/displayed brightness.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: Both human vision and most display/camera pipelines respond to light nonlinearly (roughly logarithmically), so linear pixel value changes don't correspond to perceptually linear brightness changes. Gamma correction lets you brighten dark regions (recover shadow detail) or darken bright regions without uniformly shifting all pixel values, which a simple addition/subtraction would do (and which clips highlights/shadows badly).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: Build a lookup table mapping each of the 256 possible input values through (i/255)^gamma * 255, then apply it via cv2.LUT(img, table) — a fast table lookup rather than per-pixel exponentiation. gamma < 1 (e.g., 0.5) pulls dark values up (brightens); gamma > 1 (e.g., 2.0) pushes them down (darkens).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Correcting underexposed images before feature detection or OCR (brightening with gamma<1 to reveal text in shadows), normalizing brightness variation across a dataset before training, or as part of an augmentation pipeline to simulate different lighting conditions.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Avoid as a fix for severely clipped/saturated images — gamma correction can't recover information that was clipped to 0 or 255 during capture, it only redistributes existing values. Avoid applying a fixed gamma blindly across a dataset with highly variable exposure; per-image adaptive correction (or CLAHE) is often better.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: Applying gamma correction to an already well-exposed image with the wrong gamma value (e.g., gamma=0.3) can blow out midtones to near-white, losing detail in the opposite direction. People also sometimes apply gamma correction to images already in a non-linear (gamma-encoded) color space, effectively double-applying the nonlinearity and producing washed-out or overly dark results.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: For a dark warehouse CCTV frame, table = np.array([(i/255.0)**0.4*255 for i in range(256)]).astype('uint8'); bright = cv2.LUT(frame, table) reveals shelf labels in shadowed aisles that were near-invisible at gamma=1.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_it_is: Finding the boundaries of connected white regions in a binary image as ordered lists of (x,y) points, then computing shape descriptors from those boundaries — area, perimeter, bounding box, convex hull, centroid, approximate polygon (number of corners), etc.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.why_it_exists: After thresholding/segmentation produces a binary mask, you usually need to go from 'which pixels are foreground' to 'how many distinct objects are there, where are they, and what shape is each one' — contour detection and analysis is the classical bridge from pixel-level masks to object-level geometric reasoning.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.how_it_works: cv2.findContours(binary,cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL/RETR_TREE,cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE) traces the boundary of each connected component (optionally with hierarchy for nested contours/holes), returning a list of point arrays. From each contour: cv2.contourArea, cv2.boundingRect, cv2.minAreaRect (rotated box), cv2.convexHull, cv2.approxPolyDP (polygon simplification with epsilon tolerance), and moments give the centroid.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.use_when: Counting/locating discrete objects after thresholding (cells under a microscope, parts on a conveyor belt), extracting bounding boxes for OCR line/word regions, detecting document edges for perspective correction (largest 4-point contour), or shape classification (circle vs square vs triangle via approxPolyDP corner count).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.avoid_when: Avoid on images where objects of interest touch or overlap heavily — findContours will merge them into one connected component unless you first separate them (watershed, morphology, or instance segmentation). Avoid for tasks needing semantic understanding (what an object IS), since contours only describe geometry.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.what_goes_wrong: RETR_TREE vs RETR_EXTERNAL confusion: RETR_EXTERNAL only returns outermost contours, silently dropping holes/nested shapes that a downstream step expected; CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE compresses straight-line segments to endpoints, which can break logic expecting every boundary pixel. Also, contourArea can return 0 or near-0 for degenerate (line-like) contours from noise, which then crash area-ratio computations via division-by-zero if not filtered.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|OpenCV.real_example: To find a document's outline in a photo: contours,_ = cv2.findContours(edges,cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL,cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE); largest = max(contours,key=cv2.contourArea); approx = cv2.approxPolyDP(largest, 0.02*cv2.arcLength(largest,True), True) — if approx has 4 points, that's the document's corners for a perspective warp.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: First-derivative edge operators that convolve an image with small 3x3 kernels to approximate the intensity gradient in the x and y directions (Gx, Gy); gradient magnitude sqrt(Gx^2+Gy^2) is high at edges. Scharr is a variant kernel with coefficients tuned to give more rotationally-symmetric (accurate) gradient estimates than Sobel, especially for 3x3 size.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Edges are where intensity changes rapidly — taking a discrete derivative highlights these changes. Sobel/Scharr provide a computationally cheap, noise-robust (because the kernel includes smoothing) way to estimate that derivative on a discrete pixel grid, forming the foundation for more sophisticated edge detectors like Canny.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: cv2.Sobel(img,cv2.CV_64F,dx,dy,ksize) convolves with a kernel like [[-1,0,1],[-2,0,2],[-1,0,1]] for the x-gradient (and its transpose for y), combining differencing with a smoothing weight. cv2.Scharr uses [[-3,0,3],[-10,0,10],[-3,0,3]] which better approximates a true rotationally-invariant gradient at small kernel sizes. Magnitude = sqrt(Gx^2+Gy^2), direction = atan2(Gy,Gx).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: As a building block inside larger pipelines (Canny uses Sobel internally), for computing gradient direction/magnitude needed by HOG or Harris corners, or for quick-and-dirty edge visualization when full Canny tuning isn't needed.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid using raw Sobel output as a final 'edge map' for clean binary edges — it produces a continuous gradient-magnitude image with thick, noisy responses, not the thin, well-localized edges Canny produces via non-max suppression and hysteresis. Avoid ksize=1 with Sobel when rotational accuracy matters — use Scharr instead.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Using cv2.CV_8U as the output dtype clips negative gradient values to 0, losing half the gradient information (edges where intensity decreases get zeroed out) — must use cv2.CV_64F or cv2.CV_16S and take absolute value afterward. Forgetting to combine Gx and Gy into a magnitude leaves you with directional-only edge maps that miss edges perpendicular to the chosen axis.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: gx = cv2.Sobel(gray,cv2.CV_64F,1,0,ksize=3); gy = cv2.Sobel(gray,cv2.CV_64F,0,1,ksize=3); mag = np.sqrt(gx**2+gy**2) — this magnitude image is the direct input to Canny's non-maximum suppression step.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: A transform that decomposes an image into a sum of 2D sinusoidal basis functions of varying spatial frequency and orientation, converting the image from the spatial domain (pixel intensities) to the frequency domain (amplitude/phase of each frequency component). FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) is the O(N log N) algorithm used to compute the DFT efficiently.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Some operations are much easier or more interpretable in the frequency domain: periodic noise (e.g., scan-line artifacts, moiré patterns) shows up as isolated bright spots in the frequency spectrum that are easy to identify and remove; blurring/sharpening correspond to attenuating/boosting high frequencies; and convolution in the spatial domain becomes simple multiplication in the frequency domain (useful for large-kernel filtering).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: cv2.dft(np.float32(img),flags=cv2.DFT_COMPLEX_OUTPUT) (or np.fft.fft2) computes the 2D DFT; np.fft.fftshift moves the zero-frequency (DC) component to the center of the spectrum for visualization. Magnitude spectrum = log(1+|F(u,v)|) is typically viewed; low frequencies (overall brightness/large structures) cluster near the center, high frequencies (edges, noise, fine texture) are at the periphery. A filter mask in frequency domain, multiplied then inverse-transformed (cv2.idft), implements frequency-domain filtering.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Diagnosing and removing periodic/structured noise (e.g., a grid pattern from a faulty sensor, or compression block artifacts), implementing large-kernel low-pass/high-pass filters efficiently, or texture analysis where frequency content distinguishes textures.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid for routine smoothing/sharpening where a spatial-domain kernel (Gaussian blur, unsharp mask) is simpler and just as effective for small kernels — FFT overhead and the fftshift/log-scaling boilerplate aren't worth it. Avoid when the noise/pattern isn't actually periodic — FFT-domain filtering won't help with random (e.g., Gaussian) noise.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting fftshift before visualizing/designing a filter mask means the 'center' of your filter mask doesn't align with the DC component, so a 'low-pass' mask actually passes high frequencies. Also, after frequency-domain filtering, forgetting to take only the real part (or magnitude) of the inverse DFT result, or forgetting to normalize/clip back to a valid pixel range, produces garbage images.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: To remove a horizontal scan-line artifact from a scanned image: compute the FFT, observe a bright vertical line of energy in the spectrum corresponding to the horizontal periodic pattern, mask out that line, then apply cv2.idft to get a cleaned image.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: A category of preprocessing techniques aimed at making an image more visually informative or suitable for downstream processing: contrast enhancement (histogram equalization/CLAHE/stretching) expands the dynamic range, sharpening (unsharp masking, high-pass filtering) accentuates edges, and color correction (white balance, gamma, LAB channel adjustment) fixes color casts and tonal balance.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Raw captured images often don't optimally represent the information content needed for either human viewing or algorithmic processing — low contrast hides detail, optical/sensor effects soften edges, and lighting conditions introduce color casts (e.g., everything looks yellowish under tungsten light). Enhancement techniques correct these issues as a preprocessing stage, often improving both human interpretability and downstream model accuracy.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: Unsharp masking: sharpened = original + amount*(original - GaussianBlur(original)) — subtracting a blurred version isolates high-frequency detail, which is then added back to boost edges. White balance/color correction: scale each color channel so that a reference 'white' patch (or the image's gray-world average) becomes neutral gray, often done in LAB space by adjusting only the a/b channels while preserving L (lightness).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: As a preprocessing pipeline step before human review (medical/satellite imagery), before feature extraction in pipelines sensitive to contrast/sharpness, or to normalize a dataset captured under inconsistent lighting/white-balance conditions before training a model.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid over-sharpening, which introduces visible halos/ringing artifacts around edges and can amplify noise; avoid color correction algorithms that assume a 'gray world' (average color = gray) on images dominated by a single strong color (e.g., a field of green grass), as they'll overcorrect and shift the dominant color toward gray.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Chaining multiple enhancement steps (contrast stretch, then sharpen, then color correct) without checking intermediate results compounds artifacts — e.g., sharpening after contrast stretching amplifies noise that the stretch itself introduced. Also, enhancement applied inconsistently across a training dataset (some images enhanced, some not) creates a distribution shift that a model can spuriously learn to exploit.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: unsharp = cv2.addWeighted(img, 1.5, cv2.GaussianBlur(img,(0,0),3), -0.5, 0) sharpens an image by adding 1.5x the original and subtracting 0.5x a blurred version, boosting edge contrast.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: Denoising techniques that go beyond Gaussian blur to remove noise while better preserving edges: the median filter replaces each pixel with the median (not mean) of its neighborhood, which is robust to outlier 'salt-and-pepper' noise; the bilateral filter averages nearby pixels weighted by both spatial distance AND intensity similarity, smoothing flat regions while preserving sharp edges; wavelet denoising decomposes the image into multi-resolution frequency bands and thresholds away small (likely noise) coefficients before reconstructing.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Gaussian blur smooths noise but also blurs edges uniformly — it can't tell the difference between 'noise' and 'a real edge'. These techniques exist to remove noise while preserving the structural information (edges, boundaries) that downstream tasks depend on, each with a different speed/quality/edge-preservation tradeoff.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: cv2.medianBlur(img,k) sorts pixel values in a kxk window and takes the middle value — completely removes isolated extreme-value (salt-and-pepper) pixels since they can never be the median. cv2.bilateralFilter(img,d,sigmaColor,sigmaSpace) computes a weighted average where weight = spatial_gaussian(distance) * intensity_gaussian(color_difference), so pixels across a strong edge (large color difference) get near-zero weight regardless of proximity. Wavelet denoising (e.g., via PyWavelets/skimage) applies a wavelet transform, soft-thresholds high-frequency coefficients (assumed to be mostly noise), and inverse-transforms.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Median filter for salt-and-pepper/impulse noise (dead pixels, transmission errors); bilateral filter when you need to denoise while keeping edges crisp (e.g., before edge detection on a noisy photo, or for cartoon-like stylization); wavelet denoising for Gaussian noise in scientific/medical images where multi-scale structure matters.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid median filter for Gaussian noise (it's less statistically efficient than mean-based methods for that noise type) or on images with fine line-like structures (median filter can erase thin lines thinner than the kernel). Avoid bilateral filter on very large images or video in real-time pipelines — it's significantly slower than Gaussian/median due to its non-separable, per-pixel-adaptive weighting.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Bilateral filter with sigmaColor set too high effectively degenerates into Gaussian blur (loses edge-preservation benefit); set too low, it does almost nothing. Median filter with too large a kernel can erase small objects entirely (anything smaller than half the kernel's footprint becomes the surrounding median value, vanishing).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: Removing salt-and-pepper noise from a faxed/scanned document: cv2.medianBlur(gray,3) removes isolated black/white speckles while keeping text edges sharp — a Gaussian blur of the same noise would smear the speckles into gray smudges instead of removing them.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: A family of pointwise pixel-mapping functions that reshape the intensity histogram without considering spatial neighbors: linear (contrast stretching), logarithmic (s = c*log(1+r), compresses a huge dynamic range into a displayable one), power-law/gamma (s = c*r^gamma, covered in depth under OpenCV Fundamentals), and their inverses.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Different image problems call for different shapes of intensity remapping. Log transforms exist specifically for images with extreme dynamic range (e.g., Fourier magnitude spectra, which span many orders of magnitude) where even gamma correction can't compress the range enough for display. Power-law/gamma is the general-purpose brightness tool (see the dedicated OpenCV Fundamentals note for its mechanics); this entry is about choosing AMONG the family based on the shape of the problem.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: Log transform: s = c*log(1+r) — compresses large values much more aggressively than small values, so a value of 10000 and 100000 end up close together in output, while 1 and 10 remain well separated. Power-law/gamma: s = c*r^gamma — a tunable curve that's concave (brighten) for gamma<1 or convex (darken) for gamma>1, with gamma=1 being identity. Both are implemented as lookup tables (cv2.LUT) for speed.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Use log transforms specifically when displaying data with enormous dynamic range — Fourier spectra, HDR radiance maps, certain medical imaging modalities — where even gamma can't bring faint and bright regions into a single viewable range simultaneously. Use power-law/gamma for the general 'brighten shadows / darken highlights' adjustment covered in OpenCV Fundamentals.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Don't reach for a log transform for ordinary photo brightness adjustment — its extreme compression of high values will flatten normal-range images into a narrow band near white. Don't use any pointwise transform when the problem is spatially varying (uneven lighting) — that calls for adaptive thresholding or CLAHE instead, which operate on local neighborhoods.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Applying a log transform to a normal 0-255 image and forgetting to rescale the output back to 0-255 (log(256)≈5.5, not 255) produces an almost-black image because the output range wasn't renormalized. Choosing the wrong family for the histogram shape — e.g., gamma correction on an image whose problem is a few extreme outlier bright pixels — won't fix the actual issue because gamma reshapes the whole curve, not just the tail.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: Displaying a DFT magnitude spectrum: magnitude values can range from near-0 to 10^6+; display = 20*np.log(np.abs(fshift)+1) compresses this into a viewable 0-255-ish range where both faint and dominant frequency components are visible, which no gamma value could achieve.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: A multi-stage edge detection algorithm widely considered the gold-standard classical edge detector: (1) Gaussian smoothing, (2) Sobel gradient computation, (3) non-maximum suppression (NMS) to thin edges to single-pixel width, (4) double-threshold hysteresis to classify and link edge pixels.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Raw gradient magnitude (from Sobel) gives thick, blurry 'edge regions' rather than clean thin lines, and a simple threshold either misses faint-but-real edges or includes noisy false edges. Canny's multi-stage design specifically addresses both problems: NMS thins edges to exactly one pixel wide along the gradient direction, and hysteresis thresholding uses two thresholds to keep weak edges only if they connect to strong ones — capturing faint edges that are part of a real structure while rejecting isolated noise.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: 1) Blur with Gaussian to reduce noise. 2) Compute gradient magnitude and direction via Sobel. 3) Non-max suppression: for each pixel, check if its gradient magnitude is a local maximum along the gradient direction; if not, suppress it to zero (thins the edge). 4) Hysteresis: pixels above the high threshold are 'strong' edges (kept); pixels below the low threshold are discarded; pixels in between are kept ONLY if connected to a strong edge pixel.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: The default choice for binary edge maps feeding into contour detection, Hough transforms (line/circle detection), or as a feature for classical document-boundary detection. Also a strong baseline before reaching for learned edge detectors.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid on very noisy images without adequate pre-blurring — Canny will produce a thicket of spurious short edge fragments. Avoid when you need edges that respond to texture/semantic boundaries rather than pure intensity gradients (use a learned segmentation model instead).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: The two threshold values (low, high) are notoriously image-dependent and require per-dataset tuning — too low produces noisy edge maps full of texture edges, too high misses real but low-contrast boundaries. A common rule of thumb (high:low ratio of 2:1 or 3:1, with high chosen via Otsu on the gradient image) helps but doesn't eliminate the need for tuning.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: edges = cv2.Canny(cv2.GaussianBlur(gray,(5,5),0), 50, 150) is the standard first step before cv2.findContours when looking for a document's rectangular outline in a photo.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: A second-derivative edge/blob detector that first smooths the image with a Gaussian (to suppress noise sensitivity, since second derivatives amplify noise heavily) then applies the Laplacian operator (sum of second partial derivatives, ∇²f = ∂²f/∂x² + ∂²f/∂y²). Edges correspond to zero-crossings of the LoG response; blobs of a characteristic size correspond to extrema of the LoG response at the matching scale.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: First-derivative methods (Sobel/Canny) detect edges as local maxima of gradient magnitude, which requires the extra non-max-suppression step to localize precisely. Second-derivative methods detect edges as zero-crossings, which are inherently well-localized points — and the same operator, evaluated at multiple Gaussian scales, doubles as a principled multi-scale blob detector (the basis of SIFT's scale-space).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: cv2.Laplacian(cv2.GaussianBlur(img,(k,k),sigma), cv2.CV_64F) approximates ∇²G*I. For edge detection, find where this signed response crosses zero. For blob detection, the LoG response is maximal (in absolute value) when the Gaussian's scale sigma matches the blob's radius (specifically radius ≈ sigma*sqrt(2)) — stacking LoG responses across a range of sigmas and finding scale-space extrema locates blobs of varying sizes.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Blob/keypoint detection at characteristic scales (the theoretical basis SIFT approximates via Difference-of-Gaussians for efficiency), or edge detection via zero-crossings when precise sub-pixel edge localization matters.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid for routine edge detection in production pipelines — Canny's NMS+hysteresis generally gives cleaner, more controllable results, and LoG is more sensitive to noise (second derivatives amplify high-frequency content even after smoothing) and more expensive than the DoG approximation used in practice.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Choosing sigma without considering the scale of features you care about means LoG either responds to noise (sigma too small) or misses fine detail entirely (sigma too large). Zero-crossing detection is also sensitive to quantization — on flat regions, tiny numerical fluctuations near zero can produce spurious zero-crossings unless thresholded by response magnitude.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: SIFT approximates LoG-based scale-space blob detection efficiently using Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG = G(sigma1)*I - G(sigma2)*I), since DoG is a close approximation to LoG but much cheaper to compute at multiple scales.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: A classical corner-detection algorithm that identifies points where the image intensity changes significantly in TWO directions (corners), as opposed to edges (change in one direction only) or flat regions (no change). It computes a 'cornerness' response R = det(M) - k*trace(M)^2 from the second-moment matrix M of local gradients.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Corners are highly distinctive, repeatable points that are easy to match across images (unlike edges, whose position along the edge direction is ambiguous, or flat regions, which have no distinguishing texture). Harris provided a principled, efficient formula to score 'cornerness' at every pixel using only local gradient statistics, enabling feature-based matching, tracking, and camera calibration.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: For each pixel, compute the structure tensor M = [[sum(Ix^2), sum(Ix*Iy)],[sum(Ix*Iy), sum(Iy^2)]] over a local window (gradients Ix,Iy from Sobel, often Gaussian-weighted). The eigenvalues λ1,λ2 of M describe how much intensity varies in the two principal directions: both large = corner, one large one small = edge, both small = flat. R = det(M) - k*trace(M)^2 = λ1*λ2 - k*(λ1+λ2)^2 is large and positive for corners, negative for edges, near-zero for flat regions — avoiding the cost of explicit eigendecomposition.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Detecting stable keypoints for camera calibration (chessboard corners), feature tracking in video (as the seed points for Lucas-Kanade optical flow via cv2.goodFeaturesToTrack, which is a Harris variant), or any task needing well-localized, repeatable interest points without needing scale/rotation invariance.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid when you need scale invariance (Harris corners aren't stable across significant zoom changes — use SIFT/ORB instead, which build in scale-space) or when you need a descriptor for matching across very different viewpoints (Harris gives point locations, not descriptors — pair with a descriptor like BRIEF if matching is needed).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: The sensitivity parameter k (typically 0.04-0.06) and the response threshold both need tuning per image — too permissive a threshold returns thousands of weak 'corners' on textured/noisy regions, too strict misses real corners on low-contrast images. Harris corners also cluster densely in textured regions, often requiring non-max suppression over a neighborhood to get well-spaced keypoints.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: cv2.goodFeaturesToTrack(gray, maxCorners=100, qualityLevel=0.01, minDistance=10) — built on the Harris/Shi-Tomasi corner response — finds the points fed into cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK for sparse optical flow tracking.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: Scale-Invariant Feature Transform: a keypoint detector + descriptor pipeline that finds interest points stable under scale, rotation, and (to some extent) illumination/viewpoint changes, and describes each as a 128-dimensional floating-point vector summarizing local gradient orientation histograms.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Before SIFT, feature matching across images with different zoom levels, rotations, or viewpoints was unreliable — Harris corners aren't scale-invariant. SIFT was designed (Lowe, 1999/2004) to provide keypoints AND descriptors that remain matchable even when the same physical point appears at different scales/orientations in two images, enabling robust image stitching, object recognition, and SLAM.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: 1) Build a scale-space pyramid using Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) at multiple octaves/scales. 2) Find local extrema in this 3D (x,y,scale) space as candidate keypoints. 3) Refine location, reject low-contrast/edge-like points. 4) Assign a dominant orientation from local gradient histogram (for rotation invariance). 5) Build a 128D descriptor from 4x4 grid of 8-bin gradient orientation histograms around the keypoint, normalized for illumination invariance.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: High-precision matching tasks where accuracy matters more than speed: panorama stitching, 3D reconstruction/SLAM with significant viewpoint changes, or as a quality benchmark to compare faster alternatives against.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid for real-time applications (SIFT is computationally expensive relative to ORB/AKAZE) and avoid when a deep-learning-based matcher or detector (e.g., learned descriptors, SuperPoint) is available and outperforms classical features on the target domain — modern pipelines increasingly favor learned features for robustness.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: SIFT was patented until 2020, which historically forced many open-source projects (and OpenCV's default build) to exclude it or require opencv-contrib with a flag — confusion about 'SIFT not available' errors often traces to this licensing history (now resolved, SIFT is in main OpenCV since 4.4+). Performance-wise, SIFT can produce too few keypoints on low-texture images (blank walls, sky) for reliable matching.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: sift = cv2.SIFT_create(); kp, des = sift.detectAndCompute(gray, None) — des is an Nx128 array of descriptors used with a FLANN or brute-force matcher for tasks like matching a reference logo against a cluttered scene photo.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF: a free, fast, rotation-invariant feature detector and descriptor that combines the FAST corner detector (for speed) with a rotation-aware version of the BRIEF binary descriptor, producing compact binary feature vectors instead of SIFT's floating-point ones.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: SIFT/SURF were patented and computationally expensive — ORB was created (2011, by OpenCV's own team) as a free, much faster alternative suitable for real-time applications and resource-constrained devices, trading some matching robustness for an order-of-magnitude speedup and patent-free licensing.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: FAST detects corners by checking if enough pixels in a circle around a candidate are all brighter or all darker than the center (a simple, very fast test). BRIEF describes a keypoint as a bitstring from a fixed set of pairwise pixel-intensity comparisons (is pixel A brighter than pixel B? → 1 bit). ORB adds: (a) an orientation from the intensity centroid so BRIEF comparisons can be rotated to match the keypoint's orientation (rotation invariance), and (b) a multi-scale pyramid for scale invariance.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Real-time feature matching/tracking on CPU or embedded devices (robotics, AR, mobile apps), SLAM systems needing many keypoints per frame at low latency, or any scenario where the patent-free, fast nature of ORB outweighs SIFT's somewhat higher matching accuracy.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid when matching needs to survive very large scale changes, strong illumination changes, or significant blur — ORB's binary descriptors are less robust to these than SIFT's gradient-histogram descriptors. Avoid using a Euclidean-distance-based matcher (BFMatcher with NORM_L2) with ORB — binary descriptors require Hamming distance (NORM_HAMMING).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Using cv2.NORM_L2 instead of cv2.NORM_HAMMING for matching ORB descriptors gives meaningless distances since binary descriptors aren't comparable in Euclidean space — this is a very common bug. Also, ORB tends to cluster keypoints in highly textured regions and find few in flat regions, similar to other corner-based detectors, which can leave large image areas without matchable points.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: orb = cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=500); kp,des = orb.detectAndCompute(gray,None); bf = cv2.BFMatcher(cv2.NORM_HAMMING, crossCheck=True); matches = bf.match(des1,des2) — a standard real-time feature-matching pipeline for tracking a planar marker in AR.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: Speeded-Up Robust Features: a scale- and rotation-invariant detector/descriptor designed as a faster approximation of SIFT, using box-filter (integral image) approximations of Gaussian derivatives and a 64- (or 128-) dimensional descriptor based on Haar wavelet responses.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: SURF (2006) aimed to deliver SIFT-like robustness at significantly higher speed by replacing SIFT's Gaussian-derivative computations with integral-image-based box filter approximations (constant time regardless of filter size) — making real-time SIFT-quality matching feasible on the hardware of its era.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: Uses integral images to approximate Laplacian-of-Gaussian responses at multiple scales via box filters (computable in O(1) per pixel regardless of box size). Keypoints are detected as local maxima of this approximated determinant-of-Hessian response across scale-space. Descriptors are built from Haar wavelet responses in a grid around the keypoint, oriented for rotation invariance.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Historically used when a SIFT-quality descriptor was needed but SIFT's speed (or its then-patent status) was prohibitive. In current practice, mainly relevant for understanding feature-detector evolution or maintaining legacy codebases.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid in new projects — SURF is ALSO patented (and was removed from default OpenCV builds, requiring opencv-contrib with a non-free flag enabled at build time), and ORB/AKAZE provide free, often-faster, comparably effective alternatives. Avoid expecting SURF to be available in a standard pip-installed opencv-python without opencv-contrib + non-free build flags.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Developers frequently hit 'cv2.xfeatures2d.SURF_create not available' errors because standard opencv-python doesn't ship SURF due to its patent status — this is a licensing/build issue, not a bug, and the practical fix is switching to ORB, AKAZE, or SIFT (now patent-free) rather than fighting with custom OpenCV builds.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: In legacy codebases you may see surf = cv2.xfeatures2d.SURF_create(400) — in any new project, this line should be replaced with cv2.ORB_create() or cv2.SIFT_create() to avoid build/licensing headaches entirely.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: Histogram of Oriented Gradients: a feature descriptor that divides an image (or detection window) into small cells, computes a histogram of gradient orientations within each cell, and concatenates these histograms (with block-level normalization) into a single feature vector describing the overall shape/structure of the region.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Before deep CNNs, HOG provided a powerful hand-crafted feature representation for object detection — particularly pedestrian detection — because it captures the overall SHAPE of an object (the outline/silhouette formed by edge orientations) while being relatively robust to small position shifts and lighting variation, unlike raw pixel values.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: 1) Compute gradients (Sobel-like) at each pixel. 2) Divide the image into small cells (e.g., 8x8 pixels). 3) For each cell, build a histogram of gradient orientations (e.g., 9 bins covering 0-180°), weighted by gradient magnitude. 4) Group cells into larger blocks (e.g., 2x2 cells) and normalize histograms within each block for illumination invariance. 5) Concatenate all block histograms into the final feature vector, typically fed to a linear SVM classifier.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Classical pedestrian/person detection (the canonical HOG+SVM detector), or any object class with a fairly consistent silhouette/shape where a learned CNN is overkill or unavailable (resource-constrained embedded detection).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid for objects whose appearance varies more by texture/color than by shape, or for multi-class detection at scale — modern CNN-based detectors (YOLO etc.) substantially outperform HOG+SVM on accuracy for nearly all detection tasks and have become the default. Avoid HOG on highly deformable objects where silhouette varies drastically (HOG assumes a roughly rigid shape template).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: HOG+SVM detection requires a sliding window across multiple scales, which is slow compared to single-shot CNN detectors and was one of the main motivations for moving to learned detectors. The choice of cell size, block size, and bin count significantly affects accuracy and must be tuned per object class/scale — defaults tuned for pedestrian detection don't transfer well to, say, detecting small icons.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: cv2.HOGDescriptor_getDefaultPeopleDetector() with hog.detectMultiScale(img) is OpenCV's built-in pedestrian detector — a classic example still used for lightweight person-presence detection where a full YOLO model would be overkill.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: Two more free, patent-unencumbered feature detector/descriptor families: AKAZE (Accelerated-KAZE) builds a nonlinear diffusion-based scale-space (preserving edges better than Gaussian blur) and produces a binary M-LDB descriptor; BRISK (Binary Robust Invariant Scalable Keypoints) uses a FAST-based detector with a circular sampling pattern for a binary descriptor, scale- and rotation-invariant.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: ORB is fast but its descriptor can be less discriminative under strong scale/rotation changes; AKAZE and BRISK round out the toolkit of free alternatives to SIFT/SURF, each making different speed/robustness tradeoffs — AKAZE's nonlinear diffusion scale-space better preserves object boundaries (good for objects with fine structure), while BRISK offers a tunable, scale-invariant binary descriptor often faster than SIFT with comparable robustness.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: AKAZE: builds scale-space using Fast Explicit Diffusion (FED) solving a nonlinear PDE that smooths within regions but preserves edges (unlike Gaussian blur which smooths everywhere equally), detects keypoints as scale-space extrema, and computes Modified-Local Difference Binary (M-LDB) descriptors. BRISK: detects corners via FAST across an image pyramid (scale invariance), then samples a fixed concentric-circle pattern of points around each keypoint, comparing pairwise intensities to form a binary descriptor (rotation-invariant via an estimated orientation).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: AKAZE when objects have important edge/boundary structure that Gaussian-based scale-spaces (SIFT/SURF/ORB) tend to blur away — e.g., textured or edge-rich objects. BRISK when you need scale invariance with binary-descriptor speed (Hamming distance matching) but want a different speed/accuracy point than ORB.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid AKAZE for very real-time/embedded applications — its nonlinear diffusion scale-space is more expensive than ORB's pyramid. Avoid BRISK/AKAZE without benchmarking on your actual data — the 'best' classical feature detector is highly dataset-dependent, and ORB often remains the practical default for real-time use.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: As with ORB, using the wrong distance metric (L2 instead of Hamming) for these binary descriptors gives meaningless match scores. Also, people often pick a feature detector based on benchmark papers without testing on their own image domain — relative rankings of SIFT/ORB/AKAZE/BRISK vary significantly depending on texture, blur, and viewpoint characteristics of the actual dataset.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: akaze = cv2.AKAZE_create(); kp,des = akaze.detectAndCompute(gray,None) is a drop-in alternative to ORB in a feature-matching pipeline when ORB produces too few stable matches on a textured industrial part.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: Algorithms for finding correspondences between two sets of feature descriptors: BFMatcher (Brute-Force Matcher) exhaustively compares every descriptor in image A against every descriptor in image B to find nearest neighbors; FLANN (Fast Library for Approximate Nearest Neighbors) uses approximate index structures (KD-trees for float descriptors, LSH for binary descriptors) to find near-neighbors much faster on large descriptor sets.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Once you have keypoint descriptors from two images, you need to find which descriptor in image A corresponds to which in image B — the basis of stitching, tracking, and recognition. Brute-force matching is simple and exact but O(N*M); FLANN trades a small amount of accuracy for large speedups when N and M are in the thousands, which matters for real-time or large-scale matching.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: cv2.BFMatcher(normType, crossCheck).knnMatch(des1,des2,k=2) computes pairwise distances (NORM_L2 for SIFT-like float descriptors, NORM_HAMMING for ORB/AKAZE/BRISK binary descriptors) and returns the k nearest neighbors per query descriptor. cv2.FlannBasedMatcher with FLANN_INDEX_KDTREE (for float) or FLANN_INDEX_LSH (for binary) builds an index once and answers approximate nearest-neighbor queries in roughly logarithmic time. The 'good match' filter typically uses Lowe's ratio test: keep a match only if the best match is significantly closer than the second-best (distance ratio < ~0.7), rejecting ambiguous matches.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: BFMatcher for small descriptor sets (hundreds of keypoints) or when crossCheck (mutual nearest-neighbor) consistency matters; FLANN for large descriptor sets (thousands+) where speed matters, such as matching against a large reference image database.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid BFMatcher on large-scale matching tasks (image retrieval against thousands of reference images) — it doesn't scale. Avoid FLANN_INDEX_KDTREE with binary (ORB/AKAZE/BRISK) descriptors — KD-trees assume continuous-valued vectors; use FLANN_INDEX_LSH or BFMatcher with NORM_HAMMING for binary descriptors instead.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Skipping Lowe's ratio test (or crossCheck) leaves in many spurious matches from repetitive textures or ambiguous regions, which then corrupt downstream RANSAC-based homography estimation. Mismatching the FLANN index type to the descriptor type (KD-tree with binary descriptors) either errors out or silently produces poor matches because Hamming-space data doesn't behave like Euclidean-space data.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: matches = bf.knnMatch(des1,des2,k=2); good = [m for m,n in matches if m.distance < 0.7*n.distance] — Lowe's ratio test filtering applied after BFMatcher.knnMatch to keep only confident matches before homography estimation.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: RANdom SAmple Consensus: a general iterative algorithm for fitting a model (e.g., a homography, fundamental matrix, or line) to data that contains a significant fraction of outliers, by repeatedly fitting the model to small random subsets and keeping the fit that's consistent with the largest number of data points (the 'inliers').
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: Feature matching (even after ratio-test filtering) still produces a meaningful fraction of incorrect matches (outliers) — e.g., a repetitive texture pattern matching to the wrong instance of itself. A least-squares fit of a homography using ALL matches, including outliers, would be badly skewed by even a few bad matches. RANSAC provides a way to fit the correct model despite this contamination, as long as the majority (or even a sizeable minority, depending on iteration count) of matches are correct.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: Repeat N times: (1) randomly sample the minimum number of points needed to fit the model (4 point-correspondences for a homography), (2) fit the model to this minimal sample, (3) count how many of ALL the matches are 'inliers' — consistent with this model within some tolerance, (4) keep the model with the most inliers seen so far. After N iterations, optionally refit the model using all inliers of the best model for a final refined estimate. N is chosen based on the desired confidence and the expected outlier ratio.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Any time you're fitting a geometric model (homography, fundamental/essential matrix, line/circle fitting) to data derived from noisy correspondences — feature matching, point cloud plane fitting, robust regression in general.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid when the outlier ratio is extremely high (>50-60%) — RANSAC's required iteration count grows exponentially with outlier ratio, and at some point random sampling is unlikely to ever hit an all-inlier minimal set within a reasonable iteration budget. Avoid for models with many parameters (large minimal sample size) combined with high outlier ratios, for the same reason.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: The reprojection-error threshold (what counts as an 'inlier') is a critical tuning knob — too tight, and even correct matches with small pixel-level noise get rejected, yielding too few inliers for a stable fit; too loose, and outliers get included, degrading the final model. Also, with too few iterations, RANSAC may never sample an all-inlier minimal set and returns a poor model — increasing iterations (or using a confidence-based adaptive iteration count) fixes this but costs more compute.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: H, mask = cv2.findHomography(src_pts, dst_pts, cv2.RANSAC, ransacReprojThreshold=5.0) — mask marks which of the input point matches RANSAC considered inliers when fitting the homography for image stitching.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_it_is: A homography is a 3x3 matrix describing the projective transformation that maps points on one plane (or from one camera viewpoint) to corresponding points on another — it captures perspective effects (vanishing points, foreshortening) that affine transforms cannot. Perspective transform (cv2.warpPerspective) applies this matrix to remap an entire image.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.why_it_exists: When a planar surface (a document, a whiteboard, a road) is photographed from an angle, it appears distorted by perspective — parallel lines converge, shapes are skewed. A homography models exactly this 8-degrees-of-freedom transformation (a 3x3 matrix up to scale), enabling 'unwarping' the image to a fronto-parallel view, or warping one image to align with another (for stitching/AR overlay).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.how_it_works: Given at least 4 corresponding point pairs between two images/planes (often from RANSAC-filtered feature matches, or 4 manually-identified document corners), cv2.findHomography(src_pts,dst_pts,cv2.RANSAC) solves for the 3x3 matrix H such that dst ≈ H @ src (in homogeneous coordinates). cv2.warpPerspective(img,H,(w,h)) then applies this matrix to every pixel, performing the perspective correction/alignment.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.use_when: Correcting perspective distortion in photographed documents ('document scanner' apps — warp the detected 4-corner quadrilateral to a rectangle), image stitching (aligning overlapping photos onto a common plane), or augmented reality (projecting virtual content onto a detected planar surface using its homography).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.avoid_when: Avoid using a homography to align images of a non-planar scene from significantly different viewpoints — a single homography only correctly models the transformation for points lying on (or near) a single plane; for general 3D scenes, you need a full epipolar-geometry/3D-reconstruction approach (fundamental/essential matrix, or NeRF-style methods).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.what_goes_wrong: Getting the order/correspondence of src_pts and dst_pts swapped or mismatched produces a homography that warps the image in completely the wrong way (often producing a heavily distorted or degenerate-looking result). Also, computing a homography from too few or poorly-distributed point correspondences (e.g., all 4 points clustered in one corner) gives a numerically unstable matrix that amplifies errors across the rest of the image.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Edge De.real_example: A 'scan to PDF' app: detect the document's 4-corner contour, order the corners (top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left), compute H = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src_corners, dst_rectangle_corners), then warped = cv2.warpPerspective(img, H, (w,h)) produces a flat, fronto-parallel scan from an angled photo.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.what_it_is: A specific technique for measuring and correcting document rotation: binarize the image, find the minimum-area rotated bounding rectangle (cv2.minAreaRect) enclosing all foreground (text/ink) pixels, read off its rotation angle, then rotate the whole image by the negative of that angle using cv2.warpAffine to make text lines horizontal.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.why_it_exists: Scanned or photographed documents are rarely perfectly aligned — even a 1-2 degree tilt significantly degrades OCR accuracy because text-line-based segmentation and character recognition models assume roughly horizontal text. minAreaRect provides a cheap, robust way to estimate the dominant rotation angle of a page directly from the distribution of ink pixels, without needing to detect individual text lines.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.how_it_works: 1) Threshold the image to get a binary mask of foreground pixels (text). 2) Get the (x,y) coordinates of all foreground pixels (np.column_stack(np.where(binary>0))). 3) cv2.minAreaRect(coords) returns the smallest rotated rectangle containing all these points, including an angle in [-90,0). 4) OpenCV's angle convention needs correction (if angle < -45, angle = -(90+angle), else angle = -angle) to get the actual page rotation. 5) Build a rotation matrix with cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center,angle,1.0) and apply cv2.warpAffine.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.use_when: Single-page scanned documents with a clear dominant text orientation and a reasonably high density of text pixels (so the bounding rectangle is driven by text, not noise/margins).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.avoid_when: Avoid when the page has very sparse text (a mostly-blank page with a small logo) — minAreaRect will be dominated by the logo's shape, not the page's true skew. Avoid when the document has mixed-orientation content (rotated tables, stamps) — a single global angle can't correct all regions correctly.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.what_goes_wrong: OpenCV's angle convention for minAreaRect is notoriously confusing and version-dependent — the raw angle value doesn't directly correspond to 'how much to rotate the image,' and naive use of the raw angle often rotates the image by 90° in the wrong direction or by (angle-90) instead of angle. Also, large amounts of non-text content (images, borders, noise specks) in the binary mask skew the bounding rectangle away from the true text angle.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.real_example: coords = np.column_stack(np.where(binary>0)); angle = cv2.minAreaRect(coords)[-1]; if angle < -45: angle = -(90+angle) else: angle = -angle; M = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D(center, angle, 1.0); deskewed = cv2.warpAffine(img, M, (w,h)) — a 2-degree tilted scan becomes horizontal, improving Tesseract's line-segmentation accuracy.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.what_it_is: Converting a grayscale document image to pure black-and-white (text=black, background=white or vice versa) as a near-mandatory preprocessing step for OCR, choosing between Otsu's global threshold and adaptive local thresholding (both covered mechanically under OpenCV Fundamentals) based on the document's lighting characteristics.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.why_it_exists: Most OCR engines (Tesseract especially) were designed and tuned around binary or near-binary images — binarization removes background texture/color variation and sharpens the text/background contrast that character-recognition models rely on. The CHOICE between Otsu and adaptive thresholding is the practically important decision for OCR specifically: scanned pages (uniform lighting, flatbed scanner) suit Otsu; phone-camera photos of documents (uneven lighting, shadows, glare) require adaptive thresholding.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.how_it_works: For flatbed-scanner-quality input with uniform illumination, cv2.threshold(gray,0,255,cv2.THRESH_BINARY+cv2.THRESH_OTSU) gives a clean global binarization in one pass. For phone-camera photos, cv2.adaptiveThreshold with a moderate block size (e.g., 15-31px) handles the shadow/glare gradients that a single global threshold cannot. Many production OCR pipelines run BOTH and pick whichever yields a higher Tesseract confidence score, or use Sauvola's method (a more sophisticated local thresholding variant common in document-analysis libraries) for the toughest cases.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.use_when: Otsu for clean scans (document management systems ingesting scanner output); adaptive thresholding (or Sauvola) for mobile-capture document pipelines (expense report apps, ID scanning) where lighting is uncontrolled.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.avoid_when: Avoid blanket binarization for OCR engines explicitly designed to work on grayscale/color input with their own internal normalization (some modern transformer-based OCR like TrOCR/Donut take raw images and do their own normalization — pre-binarizing can actually HURT these models by discarding information they were trained to use).
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.what_goes_wrong: Applying Otsu to a phone photo with a strong shadow gradient typically binarizes one half of the page correctly and turns the other half solid black or solid white, making that half's text completely unrecognizable — this single failure mode is the most common reason 'OCR works on scans but not on photos.'
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.real_example: A pipeline for receipt photos: try cv2.threshold(...,cv2.THRESH_OTSU) first; if the resulting black-pixel ratio is outside a sane range (e.g., >60% black, indicating a shadow swamped half the page), fall back to cv2.adaptiveThreshold instead.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.what_it_is: OCR-specific denoising: removing scanner/camera noise (JPEG artifacts, sensor grain, paper texture) while preserving the thin strokes of text characters — non-local means (cv2.fastNlMeansDenoising) is the addition here beyond the median/bilateral/wavelet techniques covered under Edge Detection & Features, because it's particularly effective at removing JPEG block artifacts common in photographed/compressed document images without blurring text edges.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.why_it_exists: Text characters are thin (often 1-3 pixels wide at typical scan resolutions), so any denoising method that blurs indiscriminately (Gaussian) risks merging or erasing strokes entirely — the choice of denoiser for OCR specifically must prioritize stroke preservation over raw smoothness. Non-local means achieves this by averaging similar PATCHES from across the whole image (not just nearby pixels), so it can smooth flat paper texture while finding and preserving repeated stroke-like patches.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.how_it_works: cv2.fastNlMeansDenoising(gray, h, templateWindowSize, searchWindowSize) — for each pixel, it searches a large window for other patches similar to the patch around that pixel, and averages across all similar patches (wherever they are in the image), weighted by similarity. Because paper texture/noise is locally random but text strokes have consistent local patterns, this preserves strokes better than spatially-local filters like Gaussian or even bilateral.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.use_when: Photographed (not scanned) documents with visible JPEG compression artifacts or camera sensor noise, especially before feeding into engines sensitive to noise (Tesseract); as a pre-step before binarization when Otsu/adaptive thresholding is producing speckled output due to noise.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.avoid_when: Avoid non-local means on large images in latency-sensitive pipelines — it's significantly more expensive than Gaussian/median/bilateral due to the patch-search step. Avoid heavy denoising of any kind on already-clean scanner output — it adds processing time for no accuracy benefit and risks softening character edges.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.what_goes_wrong: Setting the filter strength h too high in fastNlMeansDenoising smooths away thin character strokes along with the noise, particularly affecting small fonts or fine serifs — degrading OCR accuracy rather than improving it. Always validate on a sample of actual document images with the target OCR engine, since 'looks cleaner to a human' doesn't guarantee 'OCR accuracy improved.'
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.real_example: denoised = cv2.fastNlMeansDenoising(gray, h=10, templateWindowSize=7, searchWindowSize=21) cleans up a grainy phone-camera receipt photo enough that Tesseract's word confidence scores rise from ~60% to ~85% on average, where a Gaussian blur of similar visual 'cleanliness' would have dropped confidence further by softening digit edges.

6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.what_it_is: Removing the dark scanner-bed border, page edges, or excess margin around the actual document content using contour detection — find the largest content-bearing contour (or the bounding box of all text contours) and crop to it before further processing.
6|🟡 T2 Classical Computer Vision|Image P.why_it_exists: Flatbed scans often include a black border where the scanner lid didn't fully cover the page, and photographed documents include background table/desk area around the page.
